idiom_name: header + implementation pair per domain module, with prefix discipline and opaque structs
implementation_notes: C has no namespaces, so a module is a translation unit plus its public header: the .h file declares only what clients may use and the .c file defines everything else as static (internal linkage), which is C's way of making a name private to the module. Published identifiers must be prefixed with the module name (billing_invoice_create) because all external symbols share one global linker namespace, and a struct whose layout must stay hidden is forward-declared in the header (typedef struct Invoice Invoice;) and defined only in the .c file. Include guards keep the header re-includable. The classic structure remains justified for ABI-stable libraries and multi-instance modules, while single-instance module state is better kept file-static.
pitfalls: Every non-static symbol is visible to the whole program: an unprefixed name (init, util_swap) collides at link time with other modules or with libc - prefix all published names with the module name.
A struct defined in the header exposes its layout to every client and freezes it; only the opaque-pointer form keeps the representation private, at the price of an allocation step.
Module-level static state is one shared instance for all clients and is not thread-safe: per-client state belongs in a struct the caller owns.
Header and implementation drift apart easily: include the module's own header from its .c file so the compiler checks the pair, and guard every header against double inclusion.
